The Akshara Tax: measuring and removing the script penalty in single-switch text entry for Malayalam
Heap Bias: correcting size-dependent visibility bias so one phone photo of a fish heap gives unbiased length-frequency at Kozhikode landings
Speaking in the wrong voice: a measured intelligibility score for Indic-script web accessibility
WellEcho: smartphone-acoustic water-level measurement in wide open dug wells
Cost-Sensitive Plastic Sorting with Error Weights Derived from Measured Extrudate Damage (the incumbent, formalised)
prior_art_critic_reason: The one-sentence novelty ("we MEASURE the misclassification costs instead of assigning them, and train with them") dies in under 30 seconds because the student never measures the only cost that matters. PVC is deliberately never extruded (correct safety call), so the ~10,000x weight that carries the entire argument is taken from literature ppm limits — assigned, exactly like RIDX (Digital Chemical Engineering, March 2026) and every compatibility-table paper. What he actually measures is HDPE/PP/PS in PET, where the published answer is already "essentially harmless, 5 wt% HDPE even toughens rPET" (MDPI Polymers 2022, which he himself cites). So Experiment A is a garage-fidelity replication of a known-benign result, and the catastrophic-cost end — the whole claim — remains borrowed. Judge's question: "Which cost did you measure that RIDX assigned?" Answer: "the small ones." Project over. Three further independent kills: (1) the headline number is a Monte Carlo projection of usable-filament yield simulated from his own confusion matrix and his own damage curve — the conclusion is an arithmetic consequence of the weights he chose, not an observation; (2) "PVC recall 0.80 to >=0.99" is statistically unresolvable on a held-out set of ~300 images (roughly 60 PVC items; 0.99 vs 0.97 is one item, the CI swallows the claim); (3) the obvious stronger baseline — just move the PVC decision threshold, or add a reject option — achieves the same recall with no retraining and no cost matrix, and it is absent from the experimental design, so the paper does not test its own null hypothesis. Meanwhile the asymmetry framed as a discovery is the operating premise of every commercial PET line (95-98% PVC ejection efficiency is a spec sheet number) and the "errors have unequal economic cost" framing is Greyparrot's and AMP's product pitch.
feasibility_critic_reason: The entire thesis rests on PVC recall from an RGB camera, and an RGB camera physically cannot separate clear PVC from clear PET — that is exactly why every serious system in this space, including the closest prior work (RIDX), uses NIR. The stated ground-truth check fails on the same pair (PET 1.38-1.40 vs rigid PVC 1.35-1.45 g/cm3, both sink in water and in saturated brine). PVC is ~1.4% of Indian household plastic waste (CPCB), so the field site yields ~6 PVC items out of 400, and the item-level 70/15/15 split leaves ~12 test items per class — a "PVC recall 0.80 -> 0.99" claim measured on ~12 items is statistically unfalsifiable. Any workaround (cutting up plumbing pipe to bulk out the class) hands the CNN a shortcut — grey pipe texture — and inflates precisely the metric being claimed. Separately, the extruder never touches PVC, so the "we MEASURED the costs" contribution measures only the benign end of the curve (HDPE/PP/PS) while the one cost that carries the 10,000x asymmetry is still assigned from literature. The novelty sentence is therefore false where it matters, and the fallback path ("costs from literature ppm limits") lands the project exactly on RIDX plus a saturated Indian AI-bin genre.

idea: How Clean Is Clean? A Sorter That Certifies Its Own Output Purity in ppm, Using Mass-Weighted Conformal Risk Control
prior_art_critic_reason: The statistical contribution was published two months ago and the physical experiment cannot produce the headline number. (a) "A Joint Finite-Sample Certificate for Adaptive Selective Conformal Risk Control" (arXiv 2606.08517, June 2026) already delivers exactly the claimed result: a finite-sample certificate that simultaneously upper-bounds the *selected* risk (handled as a ratio with a random denominator — the precise "aggregate not per-item" wrinkle the project claims as its novelty) AND lower-bounds the acceptance rate (the "throughput price"). Selective Conformal Risk Control (arXiv 2512.12844) and weighted conformal selection with finite-sample FDR control (Jin & Candès; arXiv 2307.09291) cover the rest. Per-item mass as a loss weight is a parameter choice inside these frameworks, not an extension. (b) Headline #3, the "calibration-set size N nobody has published," is the textbook split-conformal inequality n >= 1/alpha - 1; for 200 ppm it prints n >= 4,999 in one line, and it has been in the conformal literature since Vovk. (c) K3 fatal: clear PVC and clear PET are visually identical under RGB — this is the exact reason industry uses X-ray fluorescence for chlorine rather than cameras. A Pi Camera classifier will have near-chance PET/PVC separation on transparent flakes, so at alpha=1% the conformal threshold will divert essentially the entire stream to the MANUAL bin. The predicted "10-25% diverted" band has no basis; the honest outcome is ~100%, which makes the operating curve degenerate and the demo (two jars) unfalsifiable theatre. (d) K1: Greyparrot's Analyzer already markets pre-baler monitoring that "certifies bale quality with confidence" and detects purity drops in 12 minutes, and Dodge-Romig rectifying inspection with an Average Outgoing Quality Limit — reject-to-100%-manual-inspection giving a bounded outgoing defect fraction, with Average Total Inspection as the throughput cost — has been the standard answer to this exact problem since 1929. A judge with a quality-control background retires this in 30 seconds.
feasibility_critic_reason: SURVIVES, conditionally — and it is the first idea in this family that survives K3 on its merits rather than on optimism. I tried three separate kill routes and all three failed to close: (a) "no real data by 3 Oct" fails because the 2,000-image dataset needs ZERO hardware and starts day 0, and the offline-replay design means one physical campaign answers all three policy arms — the project cannot reach zero even if every component is lost in transit; (b) "hardware sinkhole" fails because there is no heat, no PID, no thermistor, no MOSFET and no extruder on the critical path, which is exactly what killed the incumbent's schedule; (c) "no demonstrable thing" fails because the two-jar demo shows the CLAIM, not just the machine. What it does NOT survive unchanged is the arithmetic of its own guarantee: with 400 items and a 15% calibration split (=60 calibration items), an RCPS-style bound at delta=0.05 can certify alpha≈5% and nothing tighter (n >= ln(1/delta)/alpha = 3.0/alpha; 1% needs n>=300, 0.2% needs n>=1500, 200 ppm needs ~15,000). The bottom three cells of the stated alpha sweep {5,2,1,0.5,0.2%} are mathematically unreachable and the campaign will return "no valid threshold." Second, the headline claim demands a (1-delta) PAC statement that Conformal Risk Control does not provide — I verified Theorem 1 of arXiv 2208.02814 bounds only E[L] <= alpha; PAC bounds require RCPS / Learn-then-Test. The title and the measurable claim contradict each other. Both are fixable in a two-hour numpy session TONIGHT, before any money is spent. If that session is not run first, flip this to killed=true.

idea: The Lipi Gap: quantifying and closing the traditional-vs-reformed orthography blind spot in Malayalam scene-text recognition
prior_art_critic_reason: Both halves of the "fix" already exist off the shelf, and the headline framing ("first to treat orthographic variant as an evaluation covariate") is false as a general claim. (1) The "lipi-invariant Unicode canonicaliser/scorer" is a documented function in AI4Bharat/IndicNLP's `MalayalamNormalizer` — it already maps consonant+virama+ZWJ to atomic chillu U+0D7A–U+0D7F and optionally collapses chillu to consonant+virama. Its absence in a baseline is a bug in the baseline, not a discovery, so the "Y points of apparent error are an encoding artifact" finding is a known preprocessing step, not new science. (2) "Lipi-balanced synthetic rendering using free traditional-orthography fonts" is literally the existing recipe for Malayalam OCR: pottan-ocr's training config renders synthetic lines in AnjaliOldLipi, Keraleeyam, Meera, Rachana, Manjari, Chilanka, Lohit, Suruma and RaghuMalayalam — the exact SMC old-lipi font set proposed here — and the J.Imaging 2022 font-diversity paper does the same trick for Indian scene text generally. (3) Worse, the premise may be sign-flipped: the free Malayalam Unicode font ecosystem, which is the only realistic source of synthetic training data for every recogniser under test, is overwhelmingly TRADITIONAL-lipi (SMC's Rachana project exists specifically to restore traditional conjuncts), so a pre-registered "traditional is >=10 points worse" hypothesis is at real risk of failing on day 3 or coming out backwards. (4) The methodological claim of firstness does not survive a 30-second challenge: stratifying OCR accuracy by typographic/orthographic tradition is an entire subfield — Fraktur vs Antiqua in historical German OCR (dedicated ground truth, dedicated models, dedicated accuracy comparisons since at least 2014), Nastaliq vs Naskh in Urdu, and traditional vs simplified Chinese scene text (there is a 2022 paper titled exactly "Traditional Chinese scene text recognition"). The residual novelty is "the Malayalam instance of a standard analysis, on 1,500 self-collected words" — a fine class project, but at ISEF Systems Software it is an evaluation slice with no algorithmic contribution, competing against SOCP solvers and MCMC configuration-space sampling. (5) K4 also fails softly: the Sasthrolsavam apparatus is laminated cards held in front of a camera, i.e. a software demo with props, which DECISION.md's own read of the judging says loses to working models.
feasibility_critic_reason: Survives, narrowly, and only because K3 and K5 are unusually strong — but it came within one inch of dying on novelty. The near-fatal blow: the idea's own cited prior art (J. Imaging 2022, "Transfer Learning and Font Diversity" for Indic STR) already established that font-diverse synthetic training fixes Indic STR font-domain gaps. So the proposed "fix" is a known technique with a new label on it, and the headline gap in Experiment A is partly guaranteed by construction (you render a ligature form the model never trained on, then report that it fails — that is a distribution shift the student manufactured, not one he discovered). Strip those away and the residual novel contribution is: an annotation schema, a prevalence count, and a Unicode normalization step that indic_nlp_library-style Malayalam normalizers already perform. That is a workshop-note-sized contribution wearing a five-experiment costume. It is NOT killed because (a) real experimental data by 3 Oct is genuinely likely here — rarer than it sounds, and the exact test that killed the landslide idea; (b) K5 is nearly spotless; (c) the field-prevalence measurement and the stratified evaluation covariate ARE new in scene text. It becomes killed if the 1–3 Sept pilot shows a gap under 5 points AND the student declines the generalization arm in how_to_fix — at that point it is an evaluation footnote about one language, and Kozhikode-cute rather than nationally interesting.

idea: AksharaScan: an optimal single-switch code for Malayalam text entry
prior_art_critic_reason: The one genuinely new claim — that jointly inducing the coding alphabet (aksharas) beats a Huffman code over Unicode codepoints by >=25% — is very close to refuted by the source coding theorem, and I measured it and it is false. On 137k characters of Malayalam Wikipedia I built exactly the two systems the proposal compares: an order-2 akshara model with per-context Huffman codes gives 5.21 bits/akshara; an order-3 codepoint model with per-context Huffman codes gives 5.60 bits/akshara. That is a 7% gap, not 25%, and it shrinks toward zero the moment you (a) raise the codepoint model order or (b) replace Huffman with arithmetic/interval coding — the measured Huffman-over-arithmetic redundancy was only 0.03–0.13 bits per symbol. Bits per sentence are invariant to how you chunk the symbol stream; the alphabet is not the decision variable the proposal claims it is. A judge who knows information theory kills this in one question: "why not just use arithmetic coding over codepoints with a longer context?" There is no good answer. Separately, the "measured baseline" is a straw man: Dasher — GPL, shipping since 2007 — already contains Data/alphabets/alphabet.Malayalam.xml plus OneButtonFilter, OneButtonDynamicFilter and ButtonMode, i.e. a free, language-model-driven, information-theoretically near-optimal SINGLE-SWITCH Malayalam text entry system already exists and has for ~19 years. Beating Android row-column scanning while ignoring Dasher is not a result. The proposal's claim that "searching for a non-Latin/abugida extension returned nothing" is also wrong on the academic side: LM-driven unequal-cost coding for switch input was done by Tanaka-Ishii & Frank (Dit4dah, 2005), r-ary Huffman + word prediction by Kim & Rudzicz (2016), and there is a fifteen-year IIT Kharagpur programme on virtual SCANNING keyboards including Indian languages and switch user-error models (Bhattacharya/Samanta/Basu, TNSRE 2008 ×2; Samanta/Sarcar/Ghosh, IJHCI 2013; Ghosh et al., Bengali, IndiaHCI 2011; Sharma & Samanta, Hindi word prediction, ACM TALIP 2014, 43.77% keystroke savings). What is left after the coding claim dies is precisely what the proposer named as their own biggest risk: "Roark's Huffman scanning applied to a new language."
feasibility_critic_reason: Survives, but narrowly and only after amputation. The strongest kill I could build is a novelty kill, not a feasibility kill: the "what's new" sentence rests entirely on "for an abugida the coding alphabet must be optimised, not assumed" — and that exact insight is already published. The URL this idea cites as its K1 evidence (arXiv 2603.25309) is NOT an Android/Switch Access source at all; it is "Separate Before You Compress: The WWHO Tokenization Architecture" (Kusal Darshana, 26 Mar 2026), which introduces Syllable-aware Grapheme Pair Encoding for abugida scripts and reports 61.7% token reduction for Sinhala and 27% for Hindi over codepoint/BPE tokenization. That is the same mechanism (induce coding units over grapheme clusters instead of codepoints for an abugida) with the same headline shape (large win over codepoints), published five months before this project starts, under a different cost function. So the ablation the idea nominates as its whole defence — "show that switching alphabet buys more than switching code" — is now a confirmation of a known result, not a discovery. Two further prior-art holes make this worse at a judging table: Dasher (language-model-driven, entropy-optimal text entry, ~150 language alphabet files, documented button/switch modes) and Nomon (CHI 2022, modern single-switch selection with real user studies) appear nowhere in the prior-art list, and either one is the first thing an AAC-literate judge names. It does not reach a kill because (a) the composition is still genuinely new — nobody has published switches-per-character for any Indic script against the scanning method people actually use, and unequal-cost coding under a switch-press objective is not what the tokenization paper optimises; and (b) on K3 this is the most data-certain idea in the file: the primary result is a deterministic simulation over a corpus that downloads in an afternoon, with no shipping, no lab, no field site, no weather, and no participants. Killing that to keep the incumbent — which needs a hand-built heated extruder from a student with no confirmed electronics experience, 1,500-2,000 hand-labelled images, AND a materials experiment, in two domains — would be the wrong call.

idea: Malayalam on 200 bytes: a script-aware short-message codec that buys LoRa range for off-grid Kerala disaster alerts
prior_art_critic_reason: A near-identical project already placed at ISEF twice, including three months ago. Brian Heers, "Efficient Lexical Encoding of Natural Language" (NLC) — ISEF 2025 Systems Software and ISEF 2026 Software Design, AAAI prize — is a corpus-trained static lexical encoder with variable-length codes, contextual sub-lexicons and morphological segmentation of unknown words, explicitly motivated by "satellite text communication, backup/emergency low-bitrate communication systems, decentralized or post-disaster mesh network messaging," built to be lightweight for underpowered devices, tested on 1,757,861 sentences across SEVEN languages, with stated future work "language-specific optimizations." This proposal IS that future-work bullet, in Malayalam. On top of that, three of the four premises in the "what's new" sentence are factually wrong and collapse under 30 seconds of expert questioning: (1) I measured Unishox2 on a realistic Malayalam KSDMA-style alert — 506 UTF-8 bytes → 192 bytes, ratio 2.64x, versus only 1.60x on the equivalent English (155 → 97). Unishox2's delta coding handles Malayalam BETTER than English, so the claimed 3.1x script penalty shrinks to ~2x once the compressor the deployment target already runs is applied. The stated biggest risk is not a risk, it is the measured reality. (2) Meshtastic already ships this: portnums.proto defines TEXT_MESSAGE_COMPRESSED_APP, "UTF-8 Plaintext with Unishox2 Compression… The Device Firmware converts a TEXT_MESSAGE_APP to TEXT_MESSAGE_COMPRESSED_APP if the compressed payload is shorter," and ATAK_PLUGIN_V2 uses "zstd dictionary compression" — i.e. corpus-trained dictionary compression of mesh payloads is already in the same firmware. (3) 3GPP TS 23.038 Release 9 standardized Malayalam-specific national language locking/single shift tables for SMS and Cell Broadcast in ~2009, precisely to kill the Indic short-message byte penalty; the problem framing is 16 years old and already has a deployed standard. Two further self-inflicted wounds: the headline target "≤1.6 bits per akshara" is arithmetically impossible — the test alert is 81 grapheme clusters, so 1.6 b/akshara means 16 bytes for a four-sentence alert; realistic order-2 akshara entropy is 5–8 bits, and Unishox2 already sits at 18.96 bits/akshara. And "two extra spreading factors ⇒ ≥2x measured range" is bad physics: SF9→SF11 buys ~5.5 dB of sensitivity, which is 1.9x range only at free-space exponent 2; at a realistic outdoor exponent of 2.7–4 it is 1.35–1.6x, and in obstruction-limited Kozhikode terrain it may be far less. Finally the application kills its own motivation: KSDMA district alerts are formulaic, so a 4–6 byte template-ID codebook (alert type + district + colour + time) with Malayalam rendered locally beats ANY text codec by an order of magnitude — this is literally how CAP, cell broadcast and ETWS work. "Why not just send a 3-byte code?" is the first question a judge asks, and there is no good answer inside the stated use case.
feasibility_critic_reason: Survives, but only because Experiment A is pure software and needs no hardware. The closest thing to a kill is the headline claim, which I checked arithmetically and it is FALSE AS WRITTEN. Using the Semtech LoRa ToA formula (125 kHz, CR 4/5, explicit header, CRC, 8-symbol preamble, LDRO on at SF11/12): a 41-byte payload at SF11 is 1151 ms, not <=400 ms. At a 400 ms budget, 41 bytes buys you SF9 (288 ms), and the uncompressed 355 bytes fits NO spreading factor at all (SF7 alone is 543 ms). So "at fixed 400 ms this permits SF11 where uncompressed forces SF9" is wrong in both directions. Separately, SF9->SF11 is only 5.0 dB of sensitivity gain (-129.5 -> -134.5 dBm); in Kozhikode terrain (path-loss exponent 3-4) 5 dB buys 1.33x-1.47x range, not the claimed ">=2x". >=2x needs ~10.5-12 dB. A judge who knows LoRa kills this at the poster in ninety seconds. It does not kill the PROJECT because the fix makes the result stronger, not weaker (see how_to_fix), and because Experiment A stands alone as a complete, hardware-free IRIS submission whose data can certainly exist by 3 Oct. Second near-kill, and the one that is actually harder to fix: an alerts-only corpus cannot train an order-2 akshara model. ~300 realistic distinct alerts x ~60 aksharas = ~18k observations against a ~500-symbol akshara alphabet, i.e. 250,000 order-2 contexts. The model is undertrained by more than an order of magnitude, and the >=45% margin over Unishox2 would be a near-duplicate-boilerplate artifact, not a result. The by-date split does not rescue this, because government boilerplate persists across dates — that "honesty control" is currently security theatre.

idea: Shape, Not Polymer: Measuring and Fixing the Geometry Shortcut in Impact-Acoustic Plastic Identification (for the Black Plastics NIR Cannot See)
prior_art_critic_reason: Both of the project's two claimed "firsts" are already published — and one of them is sitting inside a paper the student already listed as prior art but admits they have not read. (1) The "hidden geometry shortcut" is not hidden: it is the acknowledged first-order physics of impact acoustics, stated explicitly in the student's own top prior-art citation. Applied Sciences 2015 (10.3390/app5041699) says in its abstract "theoretically their impact response behaviors were determined by their diameters and thicknesses" — and the authors therefore sieved the scraps to equalise diameter and laser-measured thickness online, i.e. they controlled the confound deliberately. So "no one has noticed these classifiers learn the part, not the polymer" is false; the field treats geometry as a known governing variable, not a shortcut. (2) The proposed fix — extract a damping/loss factor from the ringdown as the geometry-invariant material property, and condition on separately measured geometry — is a codified international standard and a 40-year-old commercial instrument category: ASTM E1876 / ISO 12680-1 / DIN EN 843-2 impulse excitation, sold as GrindoSonic and IMCE RFDA, which tap a specimen, report resonant frequency AND damping from the decay envelope, and mandate standardised specimen geometry for exactly the reason this project claims to discover. (3) The "first to point acoustics at black plastics" claim is directly pre-empted by Sensors 2017 (10.3390/s17061325), whose abstract is explicitly motivated by "black and dark dyed plastics which are very difficult to recognize using visual sensors" and which fuses impact resonant acoustic emission with 3D laser-triangulation measurement of the scraps' geometrical features — acoustic + geometry conditioning, aimed at black plastics, nine years ago. (4) The methodological contribution reduces to swapping a random split for leave-one-group-out, which is generic ML hygiene (leave-one-site-out, leave-one-subject-out, leave-one-hospital-out), and whose outcome is pre-determined by the physics: of course accuracy collapses when resonant frequency is a geometry function. Predicting a known physical consequence is not a finding. A judge who reads only the abstracts of the four papers already in the prior_art_checked list kills this in under 30 seconds.
feasibility_critic_reason: I tried hard to kill this on K3 and could not. It is the first idea in this set where real experimental data by 3 Oct is genuinely likely rather than hopeful: E1 (640 recordings on 32 cut coupons) needs one evening of bench time and cannot fail to produce a dataset; E3 and E5 are pure compute on already-collected audio; there is no weather dependency, no field site, no permissions, no third party, no living subjects, no heat, no solvents, and — critically — nothing here needs prior SRC approval, so collection can start on day 1 instead of after a review cycle. The hand-released pendulum fallback means a complete absence of electronics skill does not stop the project. It survives K3 and K5 cleanly. It survives K4 (a pre-registered, quantitative, non-product claim plus one of the best Sasthrolsavam tables available). It is WOUNDED, not killed, on K6 and on two of its four predictions: the RGB baseline in prediction 3 is a strawman, the fix in prediction 2 is mechanistically likely to fail as written, and 'we showed four low-impact papers overstated their accuracy by using the wrong split' is a quieter sentence than anything in the catalogued ISEF top-award list. Proceed only with the repairs in how_to_fix, and only after the day-1 literature check is actually done.

idea: Listening Down a Well: Where Acoustic Depth-to-Water Sounding Breaks as the Well Gets Wide, and a Phone-Only Estimator That Survives It
prior_art_critic_reason: A free, live, worldwide smartphone app already does exactly the proposed thing: the Groundwater Global App (Dirk Diederen, TU Delft / Groundwater Global Foundation, EGU 2024, doi:10.5194/egusphere-egu24-17382, app.groundwater.global) "turns anyone's smartphone into a groundwater measurement device" using the phone's own speaker and microphone, and — verbatim from the abstract — "the measurement is based on acoustic resonance." Its own public spec page runs BOTH of the project's two proposed estimators as selectable "tunes": resonance for 0.5–10 m and sonar (time-of-flight) for 5–50+ m. It already covers the diameter question ("developed and tested primarily on 2.5 cm pipes... will also work for 5–20 cm and bigger but this has not been fully tested") and already addresses hand-dug wells explicitly ("Pipes can be put in a hole drilled in the ground or they can be mounted in existing (hand-dug) wells. In hand-dug wells pick a small diameter pipe and mount it on the side"). Separately, the idea's single strongest stated evidence — "a Crossref bibliographic search returns no published work at all on acoustic depth-to-water measurement in wells" — is simply false; the method has an 89-year literature (SPE/AIME 1937, "Determination of Fluid Level in Oil Wells by the Pressure-wave Echo Method"), a mature commercial industry (Echometer, Eno Scientific), and a current signal-processing literature (IEEE Sensors J. 2025; Measurement 2022; J. Phys. Conf. Ser. 2019), plus a standing acoustic-resonance level-gauging literature (IEEE IMTC 1999; IFAC 2008; Sensors 2017; IEEE TIM 2023). A judge who types "smartphone groundwater acoustic" into a search box finds the app in under 30 seconds and the whats_new sentence collapses, taking the student's credibility with it. What remains — "where does the plane-wave assumption break as D rises through f_c = 1.84c/(pi*D)" — is measuring a textbook duct-cutoff formula (Morse & Ingard), not discovering one.
feasibility_critic_reason: The novel estimator is mathematically underdetermined in exactly the regime it claims to conquer: for a real Kozhikode dug well in September (D ≈ 1.0–2.4 m, water 1.5–3 m down after monsoon), only 1.0–3.5 axial modes lie below the cross-mode cutoff f_c = 1.84c/(πD), so there is no "comb" whose spacing Δf = c/2L can be fitted — and the modes that do exist sit at 8–60 Hz, below the project's own stated 100–800 Hz analysis band and below anything a Rs 800 Bluetooth speaker radiates or a Rs 700 AC-coupled USB sound card passes. Compounding this, the E1 rig cannot physically be built (a 1.0 m × 2.5 m water-tight cavity is not a Rs 800 drum, and 1,885 L of hand-hauled water per length sweep), so diameter and column length are confounded precisely along D/L, which is the dependent variable of the headline result.

idea: KaliDTA: a Rs 2,500 differential thermal analyser that quantifies coconut-oil adulteration from its crystallization curve
prior_art_critic_reason: Two of the three claimed novelties are factually wrong, and the third is a strawman comparison. (1) "The DSC literature uses only the single crystallization-onset feature" is false: chemometrics on the WHOLE DSC thermogram is the standard method in this exact sub-field — "Differential Scanning Calorimetric Analysis of Virgin Coconut Oil, Palm Olein and their Adulterated Blends" (CORD 2019, doi:10.37833/cord.v35i01.10) already ran PLS/iPLS on full VCO+palm-olein thermograms and reported RMSE 2.23% and 3.27%, i.e. BETTER than KaliDTA's own 2.5 wt% MAE target and on the identical oil pair; Springer Eur Food Res Technol 2025 (doi:10.1007/s00217-025-04803-0) explicitly uses "raw differential scanning calorimetry data" with chemometrics; Foods 2023 (doi:10.3390/foods12183352) and Food Chemistry 2023 (PMID 36435104) do DSC + PCA/LDA/KNN/SVM. So Experiment 2's headline ("full curve beats onset feature by >=30%") would re-derive a result that has been standard practice since the 1990s, and a food-chemistry judge kills it in one sentence. (2) "First to do this on cheap hardware" is false in spirit: a 2026 paper already puts an ESP32 + dielectric sensor + Random Forest on virgin-coconut-oil adulteration (jppipa.unram.ac.id/index.php/jppipa/article/view/13481), and cheaper/better coconut-oil-specific field sensors already hit 2% LOD for exactly palm oil and paraffin — side-polished plastic optical fibre and long-period-grating fibre sensors (Optik 2011, doi:10.1016/j.ijleo.2010.12.009), a planar double-spiral microwave sensor built specifically for coconut oil (IEEE WAMS 2022, doi:10.1109/wams54719.2022.9848037), a low-cost microwave sensor for edible oil (Appl. Sci. 2022), and thermal-lens detection of coconut-oil adulteration (Appl. Phys. B 2019). KaliDTA's fallback LOD of 10 wt% is 5x worse than fibre-optic sensors that cost less than the ESP32. (3) The DART head-to-head is a rigged fight: FSSAI's DART booklet is a consumer-awareness leaflet, not India's regulatory method. The actual legal tests for coconut-oil adulteration are the FSSAI Manual of Methods ones — Butyro-refractometer reading, iodine value, Polenske value, GC-FID fatty acid profile. Beating a visual yes/no leaflet is not a result; a judge who knows FSSAI will say so in 30 seconds, and the entire "the number no prior work reports" claim collapses because no prior work reports it for the same reason nobody benchmarks a stopwatch against a sundial. Additionally, the physical premise is shaky: the cooling-curve solidification test for fats is a century-old standard method (AOCS Cc 12-59 Titer Test, ASTM D6875 solidification point by thermistor, ASTM D5771 stepped-cooling cloud point) and automated cloud/pour-point analysers are an off-the-shelf instrument class, so "instrumented cooling curve of a fat" is not a new measurement. Engineering-wise, DS18B20 at 12-bit needs 750 ms/conversion (max ~1.3 Hz, not the claimed 2 Hz) with +/-0.5 C absolute accuracy and 0.0625 C quantisation, against a 2 wt% signal that is a fraction of a degree of onset shift on a non-linear ice-bath ramp; and 1 wt% of a ~4.5 g sample is 0.045 g on a 0.01 g scale, a 20%+ relative mixing error at the low end. The honest expected outcome is a device that separates 20-40% adulteration, which is where the DART leaflet already works.
feasibility_critic_reason: Survives, but only the de-scoped version. I tried hard to kill it on K3 and could not: this is the rare proposal where every input is a bench input — no weather, no field site, no third-party access, no dataset to beg for, no mentor strictly required, parts with 3-5 day lead time to Kozhikode. The physics is also robustly on its side: 5 mL of coconut oil releases roughly 460 J of crystallization latent heat against only ~9 J/K of sensible heat capacity, so the crystallization arrest is a ~50 K-equivalent signal that cannot fail to appear. The 9 Sep go/no-go will pass. What must die is the STATED SCOPE (140 DTA runs + 24 DART bottles + 20 market samples + 4 experiments + a 1D CNN, alongside Class 12 and KEAM/JEE) and the headline framing (palm OLEIN as the star adulterant). If the student runs the plan as written he will produce a half-finished matrix and an indefensible LOD; if he runs the fixed version in how_to_fix he will have real, clean, quotable data by 3 Oct.

idea: Water or Smoke: recovering true PM2.5 from already-deployed low-cost air sensors using their own particle size bins
prior_art_critic_reason: The one-sentence "what's new" is factually false, and a judge who knows this literature kills it in under 30 seconds. Di Antonio, Popoola, Ouyang, Saffell & Jones, Sensors 2018, 18(9):2790 — "Developing a Relative Humidity Correction for Low-Cost Sensors Measuring Ambient Particulate Matter" — states in its own abstract: "by exploiting the measured particle size distribution information rather than PM as has been suggested elsewhere, a correction can be derived which not only significantly improves sensor performance... We conclude that a correction based on particle size distribution, rather than PM mass, is required to properly account for RH effects." That is this project's headline hypothesis, published eight years ago, with the overestimation cut from a factor of ~5 to 1.05. The claim "measures for the first time how much of that correction can be recovered from the ambient sensor's own particle size-bin channels" cannot be said out loud in front of an SRC reviewer. Second, Wallace, Sci. Total Environ. 2023, "Cracking the code" showed the PMS5003's reported PM2.5 (CF_1) is reproduced as a*(N1+N2) + b*N3 + d with R^2 > 0.99 across eight sensors — the reported PM2.5 IS a fixed linear function of bins 1-3, so the only information the six bins add over PM2.5 is the N1:N2 split and the near-degenerate coarse bins, which the student's own cited RSC EA 2024 paper says are largely collinear and which Kuula et al. showed the PMS5003 barely resolves above ~1 um. Experiment 0 is therefore not an open question with a 50/50 answer; a large part of the answer is already published, and it points the wrong way. Third, Wallace et al., Atmos. Environ. 2021 already did "recompute PM2.5 in software from the sensor's own number-count channels and apply it retroactively to sensors already in the field" (the ALT method) — that is the exact deployment story. Fourth, the retrofit is a shipped product: PurpleAir applies the EPA/Barkjohn RH correction on its public map and API, and AirGradient — a company based in Chiang Mai, i.e. humid tropical Asia — applies the EPA formula server-side to every monitor and additionally offers a particle-count-based custom calibration, so "millions of already-deployed sensors have no route to this" is not true for the two largest low-cost networks. Fifth, and independently fatal on rigour: the dried channel is the ONLY reference in the whole project, with no independent instrument to verify it, while silica gel in a 40 mm tube at the PMS5003's ~0.1 L/min fan flow saturates within hours in Kerala monsoon air — the reference silently drifts, and every number in the project is measured against it. Sixth, K3: 25 hours of chamber time across 60 runs, dual-UART + dual-I2C + SD firmware from a student with no confirmed electronics experience, a 3-week unattended rooftop deployment and model training and TFLite deployment, all inside five weeks of a board-exam year. The demo (steam vs incense, two displays) is genuinely excellent and is the only part that survives intact.
feasibility_critic_reason: The project's entire headline claim rests on a hypothesis the published literature has already answered in the negative twice — Kuula et al. (AMT 2020) finds the PMS5003 is effectively a single-bin detector below ~0.8 µm whose reported size bins are not independent measurements, and the RSC 2024 study the student himself cites finds the bin counts "generally linearly related" — so the ~25-30% likely outcome of EXPERIMENT 0 is that the six bins carry no information beyond PM2.5 and the software-only correction collapses mathematically into the existing Barkjohn RH regression it was supposed to beat by 25%; compounding this, the paired labels depend on a hand-built PVC/silica-gel diffusion dryer whose particle penetration and effect on the PMS5003's weak internal blower cannot be measured with anything in the Rs 8,250 budget, and both named fallbacks are void (SDS011 emits only PM2.5/PM10 and no particle-number bins at all, so it cannot test the bin hypothesis; the hardware-dryer result is AMT 2022, already published).

idea: Touch to Diagnose: Evoked Movement Kinetics as an Earlier, Cheaper Readout of Salt Stress Than Colour
prior_art_critic_reason: It dies on three of the six tests, and the fatal one is K1 combined with K6. The stated problem — "coastal wells in Kerala are turning saline and farmers cannot see it" — is already solved, instantly and more directly, by the Rs 400 TDS/EC pen that appears in this project's own hardware list. A judge takes ten seconds to ask "why would a farmer keep 20 potted weeds and film them for a week when a Rs 300 meter dipped in the well answers the same question in three seconds?" and there is no answer in the current framing, because Mimosa pudica is not a crop and the project never links its readout to any crop outcome. On top of that, the one genuinely new-sounding element is a comparison, not a finding: salt depressing seismonasty is already published (Sapina-Solano 2024, PMID 39094481), leaf-movement-as-early-stress-sensor is already published twice (Plant Physiol 2021; Plant Methods 2025, PMID 41354977), needle-angle drought detection is published (PMID 40420859), and even non-salt nutrient stress altering Mimosa leaf movement is published (Acta Soc Bot Pol, iron deficiency, 10.5586/asbp.1996.043). The residual contribution is "we ran two known readouts side by side and one was N days earlier on a weed," where the project itself concedes the modal outcome may be a null. K3 then finishes it: 80 wild-dug, transplant-shocked Mimosa, 2,000 videos, a from-scratch OpenCV pipeline counting leaflet pairs by connected components, 25 days of data ending 1 Oct with an IRIS deadline of 3 Oct, run by two Class-12 students in a KEAM year — and the headline claim is uncomputable unless D_colour happens to fall inside that same 25-day window, which in 200 ml pots receiving 40 ml of unleached 100–150 mM NaCl daily it very likely will not (plants go from asymptomatic to dead in a compressed burst, and lead time collapses to zero or becomes censored). Finally, the genre is against it: "effect of X on the sensitive plant's closing time" is one of the most common middle-school science-fair templates in existence, and no catalogued ISEF top award or Indian placer in /Users/apple/x/dumb/dakshin/winners/regeneron-isef.csv resembles plant-movement sensing — the Indian pattern there is uniformly cheap sensor + ML + a named human/animal beneficiary.
feasibility_critic_reason: Killed on K6 + K4, not on K3. The organism is not a crop. Every framing sentence ("coastal wells in Kerala are turning saline and farmers cannot see it until the crop is dying") promises an agricultural diagnostic, but the assay only works on a seismonastic plant, and Mimosa pudica is a roadside weed nobody farms. The one thing that would close that gap — the "nyctinastic crop comparison set" — appears exactly once, in the equipment list, with no n, no protocol, no timepoints and no analysis plan; it does not exist in Experiments 1, 2 or 3. So the first question any ISEF or IRIS Plant Sciences judge asks ("how does a farmer use this?") has no answer, and the project degrades to a careful measurement about a weed. Compounding it on K4: of the two lead-time comparisons, the one likely to succeed (vs RGB colour) is a foregone conclusion — chlorosis is a textbook-late symptom and beating ExG/GLI by 3 days will impress no plant scientist — while the one that would actually be a contribution (vs the passive leaf-angle method) rests on an overnight arm that is technically broken as specified: nyctinasty requires darkness, a Rs 900 USB webcam has an IR-cut filter and no IR illumination, and lighting the plants to see them suppresses the very rhythm being measured. Kill the passive arm and the novelty ("nobody has run these head-to-head") evaporates, because Sapina-Solano et al. 2024 already published that salt depresses seismonasty. Secondary kill on CS fit: for a CS student whose stated goal is national/global CS recognition, the computational content is background subtraction, frame differencing, connected components and a logistic regression on four hand-crafted features — a weekend exercise — filed in a category where none of it is judged.

idea: The Invisible Farm: Why Global Land-Cover Maps Cannot See Kerala's Homestead Agriculture
prior_art_critic_reason: The project's central "what's new" — "these products force a hard single-class label; the correct output is a fractional cover map" — is factually false about one of the three products it audits and already operational in two others. Google Dynamic World V1 publishes nine per-pixel class PROBABILITY bands at 10 m (water, trees, grass, flooded_vegetation, crops, shrub_and_scrub, built, bare, snow_and_ice); its `label` band is nothing but the argmax of that vector, and Google's own documentation warns that "top-1 'probabilities' for predicted land covers that are in-part defined by cover over time, like crops, can be comparatively low." Copernicus CGLS-LC100 Collection 3 ships ten explicit `*-coverfraction` layers (tree, crops, urban, shrub, grass, bare...) globally and free in Earth Engine. So a judge with any Earth-observation background lands the 30-second kill: "Dynamic World already hands you fractions. You took the argmax yourself, then built a project around the argmax being wrong." Underneath that, the mixed-pixel/sub-pixel-abundance problem is the foundational textbook result of the field (linear spectral mixture analysis, MODIS VCF, Hansen tree-cover, TERN fractional cover, GLOBMAP FTC, and the RSE 2024 fractional-regression paper the proposal itself cites) — "hard classification is ill-posed for heterogeneous parcels" is a chapter heading, not a finding. And the audit half is a saturated template: probability-sample + Olofsson area-adjusted accuracy assessment of the 10 m global products has been published for Syria, Malawi, CONUS, Paraguay/Zambia/Zimbabwe, Sanjiangyuan, global mountains, European mountains and Botswana, with two of those papers pre-empting the proposal's own two rhetorical moves ("higher resolution is not always a good [thing]" and "locally trained model beats the global product"). Swapping Kerala into that table is a new row, not a new result.
feasibility_critic_reason: The headline claim is a definitional strawman, not a map error, and the ground truth is circular. ESA WorldCover's own product spec assigns perennial woody crops and plantations to Tree cover, not Cropland (Cropland = annual/herbaceous cropland); Dynamic World's "Crops" class is explicitly defined as human-planted cereals/grasses/crops NOT at tree height, and "Trees" covers dense tall canopy including plantations. So a 10 m map calling a coconut-and-areca homestead "trees" is doing exactly what its legend says. "Cropland producer's accuracy below 40% on homestead plots" is therefore guaranteed before any data is collected — it measures the student's own re-definition of cropland, not a failure of the product, and the first remote-sensing-literate judge or SRC reviewer will say so in one sentence. Worse, the reference data is 255 of 300 plots' worth of visual interpretation of overhead basemap imagery — i.e. the project uses overhead imagery as truth to prove that overhead imagery cannot see the farms. The thing that makes a Kerala homestead a farm (banana, tuber, pepper, cultivation status vs abandoned overgrowth) is invisible under canopy at ANY overhead resolution, so the interpreted "reference cover fractions" for exactly the class in dispute are unverifiable. Only the field plots see under the canopy, and 45 (realistically 15-25 after access refusals and September rain) cannot carry a design-based area estimate with credible CIs. Add claim (2), which compares a satellite-derived area against Kerala Agricultural Statistics that are compiled under a different definition and already count homestead coconut/banana as cropped area — another guaranteed number — and claim (4), where a hard classifier's error rate MUST rise with mixture entropy by construction of the label. Three of the four pre-specified claims are analytically true before the experiment runs. Separately: for a student whose stated love is computer science, the CS content is a multi-output sklearn RandomForest and a GEE composite — no algorithmic contribution at all, in the ISEF lane (Earth & Environmental) where the winner data shows Indian entrants place with cheap sensor + ML + named beneficiary, not with validation studies.
